entries.text: Men are quick to change ruler when they imagine they can improve their lot.
Men are quick to rebel against a ruler who they think can improve their lot.
A ruler who damages the interests of those whose support he needs to maintain power will make enemies.
A ruler who cannot give the people what they expected will lose their friendship.
A ruler who tries to be tough with the people he needs to maintain power will fail.
A ruler who underestimates the difficulty of holding onto a new possession in a foreign land may face significant challenges and instability.
A ruler who fails to adapt to the local customs and institutions may face rebellion and opposition from the local population.
A ruler who fails to manage relations with new neighbors will soon lose the territory they have taken.
A ruler who does not see trouble in advance will be unable to resolve issues quickly.
A ruler who does not establish colonies in the new territory will have to maintain large numbers of infantry and cavalry, which will be expensive and provoke hostility.
A ruler who fails to manage relations with their new neighbors will soon lose what territory they have taken.
A ruler who does not see trouble in advance will be unable to deal with it effectively.
A ruler who makes mistakes in other departments will undermine their position and lead to loss of allies and territory.
A ruler should be cautious not to let their enemies grow too powerful, as this can lead to their own downfall.
A ruler should not prioritize short-term gains over long-term security and stability.
A ruler should be aware of the potential consequences of their actions and take steps to mitigate them.
When you have won a victory, you can't look to any barons for help, so after it there are none around to pose a threat.
In countries run along French lines, you can make inroads easily enough, winning the support of a baron or two, but afterwards you're going to have all kinds of problems holding onto what you've won.
Conquering a city accustomed to self-government without destroying it will lead to rebellion.
Occupation can never be benevolent enough to win the hearts and minds of the people.
The new ruler's own forces should be used to conquer the state to ensure success.
A ruler who relies too much on lucky circumstances will be less likely to last.
A ruler who introduces change without solid experience will face opposition.
A ruler who depends on others to achieve their goals will be bound to fail.

A ruler who relies too heavily on the loyalty of others may find themselves vulnerable to rebellion.
A ruler who is too cautious may miss opportunities to achieve their goals.
A ruler who is unwilling to take calculated risks may find themselves unable to achieve their goals.
A ruler who is unaware of the potential consequences of their actions may find themselves facing unintended consequences.
A ruler who is unwilling to adapt to changing circumstances may find themselves unable to achieve their goals.
Do not rely on the support of others for power
Be cautious of the influence of others on your power
Do not underestimate the importance of building a strong foundation for power
A ruler who relies on lucky circumstances and positive qualities may not be able to achieve their goals in the long term.
A ruler who seizes power by crime may face opposition and challenges.
A ruler who becomes hereditary ruler with the support of their fellow citizens may face challenges and opposition.
A ruler who does not build solid foundations for their power may struggle to achieve their goals.
A ruler who does not respond to aggression with their own forces and talent may struggle to achieve their goals.
The pursuit of power through crime and manipulation may not bring glory or long-term success.
Loyalty and mercy are essential for building strong relationships and maintaining power in the long term.
A strong personality and ability to take charge are not enough to achieve power; one must also be willing to make tough decisions and take risks.
A ruler who is not drastic enough at the beginning but grows increasingly cruel later on will be seen as weak.
A ruler who is cruel on a regular basis will not be able to count on their subjects.
A ruler who is surrounded by men who consider themselves their equals will find it hard to give them orders or manage affairs as they want.
A ruler who becomes king with the support of the nobles will have more trouble keeping it than a king who gets there with the support of the people.
A ruler who becomes king against the will of the majority and with the support of the wealthy nobles must be careful not to alienate the common people.
A ruler who becomes king with the support of the people must keep the people on his side to maintain power.

It's rash and presumptuous for a remnant to discuss Church states, as they depend on forces beyond human reason.
A ruler who relies on outside help will always be in a precarious position.
The Church's power can be threatened by the ambition of cardinals.
The use of mercenaries can lead to a loss of control and a prolonged dependence on foreign armies.
The Church's power can be undermined by the short lifespan of popes.
Relying on mercenaries for defense is a recipe for disaster.
A ruler or republic that relies on mercenaries will never be stable or secure.
Mercenaries will plunder and pillage in peacetime and let the enemy plunder in wartime.
A republic that pays for mercenary armies is more likely to fall victim to a coup.
A ruler or republic that does not have good laws and good armed forces will fall victim to a coup.
